Most of the people giving this game a thumbs-up probably don't even play it anymore. A lot of the positive opinions seem to come from nostalgia or a few flashy gameplay moments. But if you actually play the game seriously, you quickly realize how many frustrating mechanics it has.

Here are just a few examples:

* **Advanced-tech wars:** The moment you reach the advanced tech era, suddenly BARBAR TANKS or BARBAR SAM launchers start spawning out of literally nowhere. No warning, no reasonable explanation — they just appear because the game wants to punish you. You can be rich, powerful, and well-prepared, and the game basically says: *"Oh, you're doing well? Let's make your gameplay poor and bad because we can."*

* **DLC multiplayer:** The game is so badly designed that if YOU own a DLC but your friend doesn't, your friend can't properly join/play with you. It's basically the game saying: *"Your friend doesn't have the DLC? Too bad. Go play something else with your broke buddy."* 

So yeah, nostalgia can make people remember this game fondly, but nostalgia doesn't magically make bad mechanics good.

If you're looking for a strategy game, there are plenty of better options. **Don't play this just because people remember it fondly.**

The game has already received plenty of positive reviews, so let's take a look at the downsides.

First off, the base game is the buggy launch version that never received proper updates over the years; the settings are buggy and limited, and gameplay almost always defaults to a Domination Victory, which is incredibly slow on larger maps since you have to annex or raze every city on the map to win.

Movement and the fog of war are terribly slow—it doesn't improve much by the late game and only gets worse on large maps.

Overall, Civ 5 is better than Civ 6 in its base state, but Civ 6 handled its expansions much better.
 The Civ 6 base game is mechanically complete, missing only the civilizations sold separately.
Civ 5, on the other hand, is incomplete and outdated without its two expansions, *Brave New World* and *Gods & Kings*. 
 Those expansions brought interface updates, countless new animations, dynamic music, graphical upgrades, gameplay fixes, a new tech tree, and far more gameplay options and variations—including multiple ways to win.
 90% of the game lies within those two expansions. 
I recommend playing at least one match without them to get a basic idea of ​​how the game works, since the game doesn't really guide new players through the added gameplay depth.

Beyond the shady practice of selling base-game updates as separate expansions, a large portion of the achievements can only be unlocked by buying them. 
 This is one of the things I hate most about Steam's policies, even though the achievement tracker correctly shows what you need to unlock them. 

 The game has many annoying issues, primarily its sluggishness: visibility is limited, movement is restricted, and every action takes a long time to process.
 You often get stuck waiting for cutscenes to finish, and the automated actions are completely buggy and limited—you have to manage every unit manually, even for repetitive tasks. 
 Movement over "long" distances simply stops working out of nowhere, and you have to manually check every turn to ensure units haven't suddenly stopped working.
 In terms of complexity and depth, *Civ* is infinitely superior to *C&C*, but regarding quality of life, it is infinitely inferior. 
 It would be a great game if you could lock a unit into repeating actions or queue up tasks for multiple units before those extremely slow cutscenes play.

 If you could choose a unit's destination and action sequence—regardless of how many turns it takes—that would help a lot. 
 The same goes for increasing the field of view and movement range, and reducing early-game construction times; nothing extreme—just +1 movement and vision for all units would satisfy me.

 Aside from the lack of any warning that the game is only complete with its two expansions, I do think it’s worth the price—expansions included. It’s a fun game, even if it is poorly balanced and extremely frustrating at times.

Sid Meier's Civilization V is a masterclass in strategy gaming that completely transforms empire-building through its tactical hex grid and elimination of unit-stacking. I love its gorgeous presentation, atmospheric soundtrack, and how features like City-States add depth to diplomacy, though the erratic AI behavior and tedious late-game unit management can sometimes slow things down. Despite those minor flaws, the hypnotic "just one more turn" loop and endless replayability make it an absolute recommendation for any strategy fan.
